chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
title: Why English audiences knew her and her decision to tour Britain
summary: Her records reached England via a German forces radio disc jockey, and after hesitating she accepted Gastel's bookings for two tours.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You mentioned that you went to England and Scotland and I don't know where else, Honolulu, you said, off the tape. This all happened after your hit record and when you went to Cafe Society in New York. You signed with Carlos Gastell, and then what happened? Did Carlos book you overseas, or what?
Oh, yes, he did, definitely. Yes, he did. As a matter of fact, I went twice, I think in one year, and it was just a tremendous success, really.

Well, my records had really -- they had known me through records for about -- well, ever since they first came out, see, because the records were released, and this was -- we're talking about like '50, '51, or something like that. And they were just warming up, and I can't remember the guy's name who was instrumental in introducing my records from Germany. They used to hear -- what do they call this? I can't think of what they called it, but it was one of those shows that you could hear records. They'd play them in Japan and they'd hear them in England.
I can't think of the name for the doggone thing right now, but nevertheless, this fellow introduced my records through that medium.
Well, it wasn't really short wave. I don't think it was short wave, but they called it something else. It was like they were playing it for the soldiers.
Something on that order, I think. And he played -- you know, would be playing the records, and the guys would hear them.

So this was how the people in England, from what I understand, got -- became aware of my records, through Germany you know. And they wanted me to come over, so I first hesitated to go. I hesitated. I don't know, I -- as I say, I guess I felt just like I did about the -- going to New York the first time. It didn't really hit me, you know, that it was -- well, that these people were aware of me. In other words, you know, I had arrived, but I guess when you take so long to arrive and you arrive you don't even know you've arrived.

So I still wasn't -- you know, it didn't excite me too much. But Carlos Castel., of course, he kept harping on it and they kept after him. "We have to have Nellie Lutcher. We want Nellie Lutcher to come. She's got to come. She's got to come." So finally, I decided to -- that I would go, and it was so marvelous, and I took my musicians with me the first time. I think we did eight weeks, and then we went back the second time and did ten weeks. And I played

all over England, and then Scotland. I went to Glasgow, Edinburgh, and did what they called -- let's see, it was something like our vaudeville here, and they didn't call it vaudeville. They called it -- what did they call the theater shows? Oh, that'll come to me too.
But anyway, everybody did that, you know. You'd play in a place a week.
